title: Contacted about a Board file, then sponsoring it
question: When a lobbyist contacts a supervisor about a numbered Board file, is that supervisor a sponsor of it more often than colleagues who were not contacted?
finding: Lobbyists wrote a Board file number on contacts about 294 files; 258 are ordinances, resolutions, motions or charter amendments introduced since 2015. Across those files a supervisor who was contacted about the file was a sponsor in 169 of 629 cases (26.9%), against 398 of 2,277 (17.5%) for sitting supervisors who were not contacted. For 3 of 33 supervisors the gap is larger than chance would give (about 1.7 expected by chance alone). A final Board roll call is on disk for 214 of the 258 files: on those, supervisors who had been contacted about the file cast 522 ayes and 14 noes, and in 521 of those 536 votes the contact was dated on or before the day of the vote.
how: A contact is tied to a Board file only when the lobbyist’s report gives the six-digit file number and the contact falls between two years before and three years after the file’s introduction. A supervisor is counted for a file when the roll calls in the site’s “Votes, appeals and hearings” page show them sitting at its introduction. “Beyond chance” is a one-sided exact test at the 5% level on each supervisor’s own counts. Ayes and noes are that supervisor’s votes on the final Board roll call of the files they were contacted about, read from the Board’s roll-call pages for measures a lobbyist cited by number (2015 to November 2026). For 5 of them the vote page lists no member and the votes are taken from the Clerk’s published minutes of the same meeting. The other 44 files have no final roll call to read: no Board vote on passage is recorded for them in those pages, or (1 of them) a vote was taken that neither the vote page nor the minutes records member by member. “Contacted before the vote” counts the files where that supervisor voted aye or no and a contact with them is dated on or before the day of that roll call; the sponsorship test itself still uses every contact in the window, including those after the vote. Whether an aye or a no was what the client wanted is tested in the screen on votes, not here.
limits: Lobbying is registered, and so is giving by a lobbyist’s clients and colleagues. The gap is the expected one and is not a sign of influence by itself: a lobbyist goes first to the member who wrote the measure, whether to back it or to fight it, so contact follows sponsorship at least as much as the reverse. Only 3.4% of contacts carry a usable file number, so most lobbying on legislation is not in this table. Most Board files pass without a dissenting vote, so a column of ayes says little about any one member. 2 files (160358, 160657) are left out wherever a final vote is counted or tested: for their last passage vote the vote page lists no member and the minutes print the action twice with different tallies, so it is not counted as unanimous and no earlier reading stands in for it. An official can sponsor or vote for something a donor wants because the official already favoured it; a donor can give to an official because of what the official already stands for. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
